newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr grounded as Kiwi takes flight.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr grounded as Kiwi takes flight.

text.p: The Australian dollar slowly lost altitude through a bumpy session Wednesday as a single large sell order caught the market long and punctured an early rally.

Traders said speculators had lifted it toward US$0.7920 resistance this morning on talk A$500 million of samurai-linked buying was in the wings. Instead, they were greeted with a A$250 million sell order out of Tokyo which sent it to US$0.7875 before a more modest A$150 million buy order provided support.
The dollar was also increasingly losing out to its counterpart across the Tasman as high New Zealand yields lured away Japanese investors who chased the Kiwi to eight year highs.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the currency was in a holding pattern at US$0.7884/89 after declining from an early US$0.7910/15. It finished Tuesday here at US$0.7883/88.
Traders said the currency was sandwiched between chart support at US$0.7850 and resistance at US$0.7950 and whichever broke first was likely to set the medium term direction.

The dollar also squandered gains on the crosses where it retreated to 86.80/90 yen from an early 87.37 high, leaving it close to Tuesday's 86.79/89 again. It took a particularly bad beating against the New Zealand dollar, sliding to a five week low at NZ$1.1266/81 from NZ$1.1376/90 late Tuesday.

Traders said the Kiwi seemed to be drawing much of the Japanese samurai demand the Australian dollar used to call its own. New Zealand's short term interest rates have been raised to more than 10 percent as part of a strict anti-inflationary policy and are expected to remain there for some time.
Australia's rates, by contrast, were cut 0.5 point to 7.0 percent in July and many analysts look for another easing if the economy does not show clear signs of a revival before year-end.
That risk had seen the issuance of A$ dual currency samurais dry up this month and bulls feared it might never revive if the U.S./Australian yield gap narrowed any further.
Sentiment on U.S. policy swung back toward a tightening Tuesday as a Federal Reserve source told Reuters that eight out of 12 regional Fed banks wanted a hike.
Domestic data so far have been too mixed to say for sure if the Reserve Bank would ease, and the same was true of today's offering of merchandise imports and consumer sentiment.
Imports rose 1.1 percent in August after a 2.8 percent fall in July, but that was below forecasts of a 2.2 percent gain.
The breakdown was also mixed with consumer imports up eight percent and capital goods four percent, but imports of intermediate goods down four percent.
There was something in this for all camps -- the jump in consumption imports suggested the strong rise in retail sales seen in July may have continued through to August.

But capital goods imports were biased up by a single plane order and down 18 percent over the last three months. That cast doubt on the government's optimistic forecast of 14 percent investment growth in 1996/97.

"Imports data are not a critical determinant of monetary policy direction, but imply domestic demand is soft enough to be consistent with another monetary easing, probably in November," said Stephen Roberts, an economist at UBS Australia.
The Westpac consumer sentiment index for September also provided amunition for the easing camp. Confidence fell 1.2 percent on top of an unexpected 0.3 percent dip in August.
However, this was the first survey since the tough Federal 1996/97 budget in August and in that respect compared favourably with past reactions to first term budgets.
"Although the budget is expected to deliver the largest contraction of government spending in recent decades, the impact on sentiment has been quite subdued," Westpac chief economist Bill Evans said.
